content:
I found out that several new problems have been added to lean-eval, such as the Jordan curve theorem.

I feel that the process of @Kim Morrison and others adding notable theorems like this to lean-eval is highly counterproductive for formal mathematics and should be stopped, along with the benchmark itself. Instead of fostering collaboration between mathematicians and convergence upon good definitions and proof methods, lean-eval is creating unnecessary tension between AI companies with secret submissions.

Instead of lean-eval, we should have a public "resultlib" – separate from mathlib but depending on it – with curated standalone proofs that might eventually make their way into mathlib or developments of specialised theories like algebraic topology. Then we can all benefit from AI.

Jeremy Tan said:

I feel that the process of Kim Morrison and others adding notable theorems like this to lean-eval

Put in another way, I feel that the problem adders are thinking "oh, I'm too lazy to start something like Carleson or PNT+ but for (say) knot theory, so I'll just chuck a new problem into lean-eval". This is not a good thought process

I've personally long desired a repo of theorem statements, and Formal Conjecture has most of the necessary infrastructure, but only accepts conjectures. Mathlib's proof_wanted isn't very suitable for this purpose, and 1000+ theorems also lacks infrastructure, so my only current choice is to add them to LeanEval. I do strive to write good definitions, and I think we might create a ForMathlib folder (which Formal Conjectures has) instead of the current approach of individual Prelude files. This would also be useful for @Kevin Buzzard's project formalizing definitions in Annals papers; specifications accompanying definitions in the form of eval tasks are certainly a plus.

Jeremy Tan said:

Put in another way, I feel that the problem adders are thinking "oh, I'm too lazy to start something like Carleson or PNT+ but for (say) knot theory, so I'll just chuck a new problem into lean-eval". This is not a good thought process

In the Annals project we are thinking "we have to formalize the statement of the main theorem in another one of these Annals papers so let's add some more definitions to mathlib" and I think that this is definitely a good thought process.

Pardon me if I missed something in the discussions, but is the objection that there seem to be many submissions which are not publicly available, but nonetheless publicly marked as 'solved' on lean-eval?

Instead of lean-eval, we should have a public "resultlib" – separate from mathlib but depending on it – with curated standalone proofs that might eventually make their way into mathlib or developments of specialised theories like algebraic topology. Then we can all benefit from AI.

I suggested something similar here - #general > New project at the Mathlib Initiative: Formal Frontier @ 💬 A more established path from AI generation through human review, edit and polish to finally mathlib acceptance is also needed before that becomes a reality. That can't happen without some sort of blessing from the mathlib maintainers, hopefully through the Formal Frontiers initiative.

I don't see a problem with lean-eval coexisting with such an effort. Different goals, different platform. The AI tokens going to lean-eval are not a problem, because there are plenty of tokens to go around. The human review cycles (that are unavoidable for any serious library formalization) are the rare resource and right now lean-eval consumes none of that.

Yes, I'm very keen to get a new library going that allows and encourages public recording of AI authored results, with room for high editorial standards, and channels for coordination between the teams contributing.

My default is that there is room for many many overlapping things here, and not all of them have to succeed.

Regarding Jeremy's original point, you will see that I have made a bunch of "let's get started on finite group theory" PRs to Mathlib lately, which were direct consequences of working on preparing lean-eval problems.

The tension between AI companies in lean-eval is very much explicitly part of the goal. It's meant to be a competition, to focus attention and elicit more work on formalization capabilities in the top models.

Another point to make here is that lean-eval consists of three separate repositories:

  • lean-eval, which is purely a problems database
  • lean-eval-submission, the current submissions and checking pipeline
  • lean-eval-leaderboard, the website rendering those submissions results as a webpage

You can do anything you like with the underlying problems database: currently it's only used for a private-submissions-acceptable leaderboard, but you can also use a it as a roadmap for a library, a test-bed for evalutating rubrics on AI generated artefacts, etc

The possible concern which I think Jeremy raised (but Jeremy feel free to correct me if I misunderstood) is that if someone wanted to work towards a 'big' theorem like Jordan curve, but then discovers it has been publicly declared 'solved' on lean-eval, and yet there is no public artifact to even inspect, let alone build upon. What will become of important tasks like Jordan curve in the long run? The incentive for humans, with or without AI, to work on these things would be greatly diminished, yet no one in the community has really benefitted from it (well, I guess except the private submitter, but surely there are diminishing returns here, as the 'solved' number increases by the same amount, namely 1, yet the problems have gotten more difficult).

I want to reject arguments like this -- Gouezel suggested a similar thing about Mazur's theorem: if it became a target for AI then it would be less likely to make it to mathlib. My counter-argument is that mathlib is glacial and we could easily list 100 theorems which we'd love in mathlib and if we continue to live in the fantasy world where we just wait for this to happen organically then we'll be waiting 100 years.

Oh I wholeheartedly agree, but I felt like Jeremy's point was about the existence of secret submissions, which certainly have zero chance of making it to mathlib or anywhere else. Unless the objective is just to convince people that it can be done; though I feel like not many need to be convinced of this, they just need the right incentives to do so, and indeed lean-eval is one such incentive, but it's not the final destination. (Hence Jeremy's suggestion of a public "resultlib".) Also, unless there's something I missed, e.g. submissions will be made public (or at least semi-public) after some specified period of time.

Junyan Xu said:

I've personally long desired a repo of theorem statements, and Formal Conjecture has most of the necessary infrastructure, but only accepts conjectures. Mathlib's proof_wanted isn't very suitable for this purpose, and 1000+ theorems also lacks infrastructure, so my only current choice is to add them to LeanEval. I do strive to write good definitions, and I think we might create a ForMathlib folder (which Formal Conjectures has) instead of the current approach of individual Prelude files. This would also be useful for Kevin Buzzard's project formalizing definitions in Annals papers; specifications accompanying definitions in the form of eval tasks are certainly a plus.

Contrary to what the name would suggest Formal Conjectures also accepts Theorems in the Category "Research Solved".
They have strict policy for accepting solved problems.

Junyan Xu said:

Mathlib's proof_wanted isn't very suitable for this purpose

I never undestoof why proof_wanted cannot be used as a "wishlist".

You mean most reviewers don't consider "wishlist" a legit use of proof_wanted?
I guess my main complaints about proof_wanted are that they don't appear in the docs and can't be referenced by other decls.

Junyan Xu said:

can't be referenced by other decls

I'm not sure this is still true, see Kim Morrison's PRs in Batteries

Junyan Xu said:

I guess my main complaints about proof_wanted are that they don't appear in the docs and can't be referenced by other decls.

These two complaints are actually facts that make utilizing proof_wanted safe.
I mean, I couldn't care less about the autogenerated docs, but many people read them — if proof_wanted items were to appear in them, they should be very clearly distinguished from theorems!

I'm not sure this is still true, see Kim Morrison's PRs in Batteries

Yeah, should have said "my complaints were". It got better after my complaint #Model comparisons for Lean > Is lean-eval worth it? @ 💬 on May 30.
